questions.q: Name the four personality types proposed by Hippocrates and the bodily humour associated with each type.
questions.a: The four types are: Sanguine (blood — cheerful, optimistic), Phlegmatic (phlegm — calm, sluggish), Melancholic (black bile — sad, depressive), Choleric (yellow bile — angry, irritable). A wrong answer (e.g., confusing humours or adding a fifth type) reveals the student has memorised names without linking each type to its specific humour, which is the core of Hippocrates' theory.

questions.q: A student writes: "In Ayurveda, a person with dominant vata dosha is calm, grounded, and gains weight easily." Is this statement correct? Explain why or why not using the Charak Samhita classification.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. Vata dosha (air/space) is associated with creativity, anxiety, irregular digestion, and a thin/light body build — not calmness or weight gain. Calm, grounded, weight-gain tendencies describe kapha dosha (earth/water). This error reveals the student has confused the three doshas' behavioural and physical correlates, a common mistake when memorising without understanding the elemental basis (vata=air, pitta=fire, kapha=earth).

questions.q: Rohan is a national-level sprinter with a rectangular, muscular build, high energy, and courage. His sister Riya is a poet with a thin, fragile frame, prefers solitude, and is described as "brainy and artistic." Using Sheldon's somatotype theory, classify each sibling and justify your classification with two behavioural descriptors per type.
questions.a: Rohan: Mesomorph — strong musculature, rectangular build; behavioural descriptors: energetic, courageous. Riya: Ectomorph — thin, long, fragile build; behavioural descriptors: introverted, artistic. A wrong classification (e.g., calling Rohan endomorph) shows the student cannot map body-build descriptors to behavioural temperaments, missing Sheldon's core claim of body-temperament covariation.

questions.q: Compare Jung's introversion-extraversion typology with Friedman & Rosenman's Type A-Type B classification on two dimensions: (a) theoretical basis (what drives the classification), and (b) health implication. Which theory has stronger empirical support for predicting coronary heart disease?
questions.a: (a) Jung: basis = direction of psychic energy (inward vs outward); no inherent health claim. Friedman & Rosenman: basis = stress-response pattern and behavioural style; explicit health claim (Type A → higher CHD risk). (b) Type A/B has stronger empirical support for CHD prediction (though later research nuanced this). A student who says "both predict health equally" or "Jung predicts CHD" confuses a structural theory of consciousness with a behavioural-risk-factor model.

questions.q: Critique the statement: "Sheldon's somatotypes are scientifically valid because body build determines personality." Use the NCERT's own evaluation and modern psychological perspective.
questions.a: The statement is flawed. NCERT explicitly states these typologies are "simple, have limited use in predicting behaviour," and "more like stereotypes." Modern psychology rejects biological determinism of body→personality; somatotypes lack reliability (inter-rater agreement low) and validity (no consistent trait correlations). A student endorsing the statement shows uncritical acceptance of a discredited theory, missing NCERT's cautionary note.

questions.q: Design a 4-item mini-questionnaire (two items per type) that could differentiate Type C (cancer-prone) from Type D (depression-prone) personalities based on their defining behavioural markers. Explain the theoretical rationale for each item.
questions.a: Type C items: (1) "I rarely express anger even when treated unfairly" (suppressed negative affect); (2) "I prioritise others' needs over my own to avoid conflict" (compliance/unassertiveness). Type D items: (1) "I often feel hopeless about the future" (negative affectivity); (2) "I avoid social situations because I fear rejection" (social inhibition). Rationale: Type C = suppression + compliance; Type D = negative affectivity + social inhibition. A poor answer mixes markers (e.g., giving Type C an item about hopelessness), showing confusion between the two extensions.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Type approaches to personality categorise individuals into discrete, qualitatively distinct groups (types) based on shared constellations of behavioural, physiological, or temperamental ______, where each type represents a broad pattern rather than a continuous dimension.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a school counsellor and two students walk in: one is constantly rushing, ______, and gets angry when delayed; the other is relaxed, easy-going, and never seems stressed.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can accurately compare and contrast at least four major type theories (Hippocrates, Ayurveda/Charak Samhita, Sheldon, Jung, Friedman & Rosenman), explain the core logic of typological classification versus trait dimensionality, and identify the key limitation that human behaviour rarely fits neatly into mutually exclusive.
